title: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day
hook: the service retells the high priest entering the holy of holies

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kittel, white like angels and like shrouds. Your line was dressed in white. Today, another man in white, long ago.

Late on Yom Kippur morning, something unusual happens in many synagogues. The prayer leader begins to tell a story. Not pray it: tell it, step by step, like a narrator. At certain lines, the whole congregation does something seen only in these Days of Awe: they get down on their knees and bow their foreheads to the floor. The story is about one man, in one room, on one day of the year, in a Temple that no longer stands.
screen: `THE LEADER TELLS A STORY.` → `FOREHEADS TO THE FLOOR.` → `ONE MAN, ONE ROOM, ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: This is the Avodah, the service: a poetic retelling of the high priest's work on Yom Kippur, based on Leviticus sixteen and the Mishnah's tractate Yoma. The Torah's rule was strict. The high priest could enter the innermost room of the sanctuary, the holy of holies, only on this day, once in the year. The day was long and exacting. The Mishnah says he immersed his body five times, moving between golden garments and simple white linen, which he wore for the holiest parts. He confessed three times: for himself and his household, then for the priests, then for all Israel. In those confessions he spoke God's four-letter name aloud, the Name itself. The Mishnah says that when the people in the courtyard heard it, they knelt, bowed, fell on their faces, and called out: blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. That's the moment congregations reenact on the floor today. Then he went in alone, carrying burning coals and incense, into a small dark room. And the Mishnah preserves a detail: coming out, he said only a short prayer in the outer room, and didn't linger, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside. Everyone was holding their breath. The Torah gives the purpose: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." When he came out safely, the Mishnah adds, he made a feast for his friends. With no Temple today, words take the place of the service, and once a year the whole room tells the story.
screen: `AVODAH: THE SERVICE.` · `WHITE LINEN, FIVE IMMERSIONS.` · `THE NAME, AND FACES ON THE FLOOR.` · `A SHORT PRAYER COMING OUT.` · then, large: `ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Go back to a moment in your life that felt set apart, a birth, a death, a vow, a silence under a huge sky, something that happened once and couldn't be repeated: where were you standing, what did the air feel like, who was waiting outside? If you pray, you can thank God for it; if not, let it be holy again for a minute, without explaining it.
Avodah. Service. The Yom Kippur retelling of the high priest's day, when congregations bow to the floor at the sound of the Name.
Your line: once a year. One man, one room, one day. That's day six hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: During the Musaf service of Yom Kippur, the prayer leader chants the Avodah, a poetic account of the high priest's service, and in many Ashkenazi congregations worshippers kneel and bow fully to the floor when the high priest's confession is recalled.

chat.says: Why do people kneel on the floor during one part of the Yom Kippur service?
options: The Avodah retells how the people bowed when the high priest spoke God's Name.
They kneel to mourn the Temple, as they do at every daily service.
They kneel because the Torah scrolls are carried around the room then.
chat.meaning: The Mishnah says the people in the courtyard knelt and bowed when they heard the Name; congregations reenact that moment in the Avodah.

notes: Five changes of clothing and five immersions (Mishnah Yoma 3:3–4); three confessions with the Name; the people's response (6:2); short prayer (5:1); feast (7:4); confirm.
Full prostration during the Avodah is mainly Ashkenazi practice; Sephardi customs differ.
'Nearly two thousand years' since the Temple's destruction (70 CE): confirm phrasing.
